paragraphs: Engineers building in the far north long relied on a simple rule: ground that stays frozen year-round is as firm as rock, so a structure set upon it needs only modest foundations. Warming has undermined this assumption. Where ice-rich permafrost thaws, the ground subsides unevenly, and houses that once stood level now lean. Some officials attribute the damage chiefly to poor construction, but the pattern of failures, which tracks local temperature records closely, argues against that view. It seems likely that foundations will increasingly need to be built to cool the ground rather than merely rest on it, for example by using thermal pipes that carry heat away, though the long-term performance of such devices remains untested. For now, the safest course is to monitor ground temperature before any building is designed.
